hypotheses.statement: When steel prices rose in 2021-2023, repeat-order prices and the invoice uplift (presumably a surcharge) lagged material cost, so contribution fell. Material on jobs shipped in 2021-2023 takes a larger share of the PO price than in 2016-2020, the extra share is concentrated in carbon-steel repeat parts whose PO price did not change, and invoice uplifts recovered only a small part of it.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: GL material/revenue was 0.275-0.315 in 2016-2020 but 0.417 in 2021 and 0.377 in 2022 (q91). Material above a 30% share was $3,058,571 in 2021, $2,524,386 in 2022 and $1,153,678 in 2023, and $501,856-$636,897 in 2024-2025 (q91). Carbon steel paid rose from $0.313/lb in 2020 to $0.508 in 2021 and $0.591 in 2022 (q78). For parts ordered in consecutive years, the median price ratio was 1.0 in 2021 and 1.1979 in 2022 (q79). Invoice uplift was $256,468 in 2021 and $598,596 in 2022 (q77), which is 0.084 and 0.237 of the material above 30% (q97). Interpretation: GL material is expensed when ordered (orient q59), so part of the gap is timing. The order of magnitude is still $1-3M a year in a cost spike and about $0.5M a year since.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: Sized from queries: about $2.5-3.1M/yr in 2021-2022, about $0.5-0.6M/yr in 2024-2025 (q91, q97). The 30% baseline is my assumption.
hypotheses.support: Job-level material cost (PO amount) divided by shipped value rises in 2021-2022 mainly on repeat parts with an unchanged unit_price. The uplift appears on only a minority of those invoices. Contribution per job falls in step with FRED steel prices, with a lag of a few months.
hypotheses.weaken: Job-level material share (POs joined to the job's shipped revenue) stays flat, so the GL gap would be timing (material ordered in 2021 for 2022 shipments) or inventory build. Or prices on repeat parts reset within one or two orders after the steel rise.

hypotheses.statement: A growing share of hourly paid time is not clocked to any job, and the growth is concentrated in particular roles or employees rather than spread evenly. Unclocked share = timecard hours minus labour-entry hours, divided by timecard hours.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: unclocked hours rose from 40,400 (0.245 of paid) in 2016 to 59,559 (0.349) in 2024 and 56,928 (0.344) in 2025 (q89). At the 2025 median rate of $25.88/h (q87), 2025 unclocked time is $1,473,297 (q98). The growth since 2016, priced at the 2024 median rate, is about $490,087/yr (q98). Interpretation: some unclocked time is legitimate indirect work (maintenance, training, material handling), so only the growth or the outliers are a possible loss.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: Sized from queries: about $1.47M/yr unclocked in 2025, of which about $0.49M/yr is growth since 2016 (q89, q98). Uses median rates, not each person's rate, and excludes benefits.
hypotheses.support: The rise comes from a subset of employees or roles whose clocked/paid ratio falls over time, while job volume and hours per job stay steady. Or unclocked time rises in weeks with low job load, which would point to idle capacity.
hypotheses.weaken: Unclocked share is similar across employees in a role and tracks a known change such as more first-article work, training of new hires (hires peaked in 2021, orient q69) or the 2025 stop in overtime. Or the gap is an artefact of week alignment: timecards are 5-working-day blocks and match labour on 34,553 of 37,813 employee-weeks (orient q34, q36).

hypotheses.statement: New-part quotes that 'expire' (no reply from the buyer) are mostly business that could have been won with follow-up. Testable form: expired new quotes are not systematically priced higher or quoted on longer lead times than won ones, and the same customers later order the same part_id from Wendlow, or send another RFQ for it.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: new quotes by status, total quoted value over the 10 years: expired 5,153 quotes / $41,451,607; lost 2,223 / $16,496,640; no award 808 / $6,100,818; won 2,764 / $20,467,328 (q88). Not-won new quote value averages $6,404,907/yr; won value is 0.242 of all decided new-quote value (q98). New parts become repeat work: requotes are won 11,818 of 12,441 times (orient q14), so each new win carries future revenue. Interpretation: winning even a few percent more of expired value is worth hundreds of thousands a year.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: Sized from queries: about $4.1M/yr of expired quoted value (q88). A recovery of a few percent would be $0.1-0.4M/yr in first-year revenue, before repeat orders. The recovery rate is a guess.
hypotheses.support: Expired quotes look like won ones on price per estimated hour and lead weeks. Customers whose quotes expire keep ordering other parts (still active). Expired quotes cluster where RFQ volume was high and quoting slow, for example quote sent long after RFQ received.
hypotheses.weaken: Expired quotes are priced well above, or quoted on longer lead weeks than, comparable won quotes, which would mean the buyer chose silently on price. Or expiry concentrates in customers who order rarely overall (tyre-kickers). The data can't say why, so this weakens but can't refute a follow-up effect.

hypotheses.statement: Routing estimates outside welding are systematically too high, so new-part quotes are priced above what the work costs, which lowers the new-quote hit rate. Testable form: on won new parts, actual/estimated hours is below 1 at laser, brake, mill, lathe, paint and assembly. Among new quotes, those with more estimated hours per dollar of material (the overestimated work centres) win less often.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: actual clocked hours / job-routing estimated hours is 0.722 (lathe) to 0.874 (assembly), 1.0 at weld and 1.062 at inspect (q80). Weld carries 483,912 of the estimated hours (q80). The new-quote win share of decided value is 0.242 (q98). Interpretation: if quotes carry roughly 20% excess hours at most work centres, Wendlow may be pricing itself out of new work. The job-routing estimate is not the quote estimate, though; conventions differ (orient q53, q54).
hypotheses.dollars_rough: Rough, partly inferred: the stake is the $1,649,664/yr lost and $4,145,161/yr expired new-quote value (q88). If overpricing explains a few points of hit rate, that is about $0.1-0.5M/yr of first-year revenue.
hypotheses.support: Quote est_hours per piece, against actual hours per piece on the matched later jobs (customer+part matching, orient q13), runs high at the same work centres. Hit rate falls as the labour share of the quoted price rises, within customer and year.
hypotheses.weaken: Quote-stage hours match actuals even though job routings don't, which would mean the routing estimate is padded, not the quote. Or hit rate doesn't vary with labour intensity. Or actuals are low only because work_date posting truncates hours (orient q40-q42).

hypotheses.statement: Scrap value is concentrated, not spread evenly: a small set of part families, work centres or employees accounts for most of the 'dimension out of tolerance' and 'operator error' scrap. Testable form: the top 10% of parts (or of op/work-centre combinations) carry more than half of scrapped value.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: scrap reports valued at the PO unit price total $756,863/yr over 10 years (q96, q98). Dimension out of tolerance is $308,074/yr and operator error $163,601/yr (q96). The GL scrap memo is $165,234-$346,419/yr at material cost (q76). Rework hours are small: 649-868 h/yr (q86). Interpretation: the material loss is in the low hundreds of thousands, plus lost capacity and late remakes. Concentration would make it fixable.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: Sized from queries: $0.17-0.35M/yr material (GL memo, q76); about $0.76M/yr at selling price (q96, q98).
hypotheses.support: A Pareto by part_id, family, work centre or employee shows heavy concentration that persists year to year. Scrap per piece run is higher on first runs of a part, after a revision, or for recently hired employees.
hypotheses.weaken: Scrap rate per piece is roughly uniform across parts, work centres and employees after allowing for volume (the Pareto just follows volume). Or the concentration moves randomly from year to year. Note that scrap is booked where it is found, not where it is caused (orient q46), so a work-centre view is limited.

hypotheses.statement: Material POs with no receipt are cancelled, duplicate or re-ordered buys that are still charged as material cost. Testable form: jobs with an unreceived material PO also have a received PO of the same material and similar pounds, and the GL material line includes the unreceived amounts.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: unreceived material POs total $149,699-$354,255 a year (q99), with the highest in 2025 (q78, q98). That is roughly 28-30% of material POs by count (orient q49). GL material equals PO amounts by order year (orient q59). Interpretation: if these are duplicates, material cost is overstated (a books problem) or material was paid for but never arrived (a cash problem). If they are small drops filled from stock, there is no loss.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: Sized from queries: $0.15-0.35M/yr of unreceived material PO value (q99).
hypotheses.support: Unreceived POs sit on jobs that also have a received PO of the same material and similar pounds. Jobs with an unreceived PO consumed no more material than comparable jobs. Vendor payments (not in the warehouse) would also be needed.
hypotheses.weaken: Unreceived POs are on jobs with no other PO for that material, and those jobs shipped, so material arrived without a receipt record (a receiving-entry gap, not a loss). Or the unreceived share is even across vendors and materials, suggesting a systematic receiving practice.

hypotheses.statement: Late payment is concentrated in a few customers, and Wendlow carries materially more receivables than its terms imply. Testable form: a minority of customers accounts for most dollar-days past due, and their lateness persists across years.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: for invoices dated 2016-2024 (265 customers), amount-weighted days past due average 18.1. That is about $1,414,984 of extra receivables, $113,199/yr at an assumed 8% cost of capital. 28 customers averaging over 30 days late carry 0.412 of overdue dollar-days (q95). Short payments are $10,071-$28,780/yr (q83). Interpretation: tens to low hundreds of thousands a year in carrying cost, plus cash tied up of about $1.4M.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: Sized from queries: about $0.11M/yr carrying cost on about $1.4M of excess AR (q95), plus $0.01-0.03M/yr in short payments (q83). The 8% rate is my assumption.
hypotheses.support: The same customers are late year after year, and lateness doesn't depend on invoice size or on season. Short payments concentrate in the same customers.
hypotheses.weaken: Lateness is spread evenly across customers, or is mostly a few days (the due_on working-day conversion, orient q17, may set due dates earlier than the customer's calendar-day terms). Or it is driven by a single year.

hypotheses.statement: Estimators' new-quote hit rates differ because of how they quote, not only because of which customers or years they quoted. Testable form: after adjusting for customer segment, customer and year, hit rates still differ by more than 5 points between estimators with at least 100 quotes.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: new-quote hit rate by estimator ranges from 0.161 (estimator 118, 124 quotes, 2021-2022) and 0.172 (115, 430 quotes) to 0.296 (327, 847 quotes) and 0.265 (108, 4,223 quotes) (q84). Expired share ranges from 0.38 to 0.669 (q84). The three lowest-hit estimators (113, 115, 118) quoted $516,139/yr of new-part value (q99). Interpretation: if the gaps are real, the recoverable value is modest. If they come from mix (estimator 118 worked only in 2021-2022, when total quotes fell, orient q11), this is fine. A pattern worth a conversation, not a judgement on anyone.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: Inferred: a few points of hit rate on $516,139/yr of quoted value (q99) is tens of thousands of dollars a year in first-year revenue.
hypotheses.support: Gaps persist within customer and year. Lower-hit estimators quote systematically higher price per estimated hour, or longer lead weeks, on similar parts.
hypotheses.weaken: Gaps vanish once customer and year are controlled for, or are within sampling noise for the small estimators (79-430 quotes).

hypotheses.statement: Some customers or part families are unprofitable once material and clocked labour are charged, and the plant-wide total hides them. Testable form: some customers with meaningful revenue have (revenue - material POs) per clocked hour well below the shop's average.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: by segment, material share of revenue is 0.325-0.346 and (revenue - material)/clocked hour is $159.4-$167.6. No customer is below $60 per clocked hour (q90). Interpretation: at segment and customer level this looks fine, and I expect the hypothesis to fail. It is worth testing by part family, order quantity and year (small-quantity orders, steel-spike years), where averages can hide losses.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: Rough, inferred: probably small. If a decile of revenue ran 20% below average value-add per hour, that would be a few hundred thousand dollars a year; nothing found yet (q90).
hypotheses.support: A tail of part families, small-quantity orders or customers has value-add per hour below the fully loaded labour-plus-overhead rate (GL direct+indirect labour+overhead+benefits / clocked hours), and it persists across years.
hypotheses.weaken: The distribution by customer, family and quantity band stays tight around the average, as it does by segment.

hypotheses.statement: Late shipments are driven mainly by late material receipts, not by plant capacity. Testable form: within the same year and part family, jobs with a receipt after the PO due date ship late against promise far more often, and the 2016 and 2021 lateness spikes coincide with late receipts rather than with high clocked load.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: late-vs-promise rate was 0.1487 in 2016 and 0.2121 in 2021, against 0.0289-0.0508 in other years (q81). In 2021 the late-ship rate was 0.7506 for jobs with a late receipt (401 jobs) vs 0.1835 for those without (7,552); in 2019 it was 0.3618 vs 0.0146 (q92). Expedited freight is billed to customers in full (q82), and customer loss is small (q85). Interpretation: the direct dollars are small: overtime premium was about $60,338 in its peak year (q98) and premium freight is $1,729-$31,223/yr in the GL (q76). The cost is mostly customer goodwill and chase work. Even 2021 non-late-receipt jobs were late 0.1835 of the time, so receipts can't be the whole story.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: Sized from queries: direct cost is small, about $0.03-0.1M/yr in a bad year (overtime premium plus premium freight, q76, q98). Indirect goodwill can't be priced from these records.
hypotheses.support: The late-receipt effect holds within year, customer and family, and the receipt delay precedes the ship delay by about the remaining routing time.
hypotheses.weaken: Jobs with late receipts are also the larger or more complex jobs (more POs, more operations), and the effect disappears once those are controlled for. Or the 2021 lateness among on-time-receipt jobs (0.1835) carries most of the late shipments, which would point to capacity or labour.

hypotheses.statement: Jobs are sometimes released to the floor on a superseded drawing revision, and these jobs account for most 'wrong revision' scrap and fit or dimension returns. Testable form: jobs whose revision_issued is older than the latest revision received (not just released) by the job's release date have much higher wrong-revision scrap and return rates.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: 'wrong revision' scrap is 137 reports but 2,852 pieces, worth $563,018 at PO price over 10 years ($56,302/yr) (q96). All credit memos average $38,189/yr (q99). Among returns, 'does not fit', 'wrong dimensions' and 'nonconforming' carry $108,018, $84,086 and $123,053 of credits (q93; RA-to-invoice joins may double-count partial shipments). Revision_issued matches the latest released revision on 32,214 of 32,372 jobs (orient q26). Interpretation: the gap between receiving and releasing a revision (orient q28) is a window in which work can start on the old drawing.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: Sized from queries: about $0.06M/yr wrong-revision scrap (q96) plus part of the $38,189/yr of credits (q99).
hypotheses.support: Wrong-revision scrap and returns sit on jobs released between a revision's received_on and released_on, or on the 158 mismatched jobs, at rates well above other jobs.
hypotheses.weaken: Wrong-revision scrap occurs on jobs whose revision_issued was current, which would point to the floor using old prints, not release lag. Or it is spread randomly relative to revision timing.

hypotheses.statement: Freight, and expedited freight in particular, is not fully billed through to customers, leaking money each year. Testable form: invoice freight is less than shipment freight on a meaningful share of shipments, or premium freight in the GL exceeds expedited freight billed.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: shipment freight is $642,130-$918,101/yr (q81). On every invoice, billed freight equals shipment freight: 0 under-billed shipments in every year and method, including expedited LTL ($103,598 in 2021) (q82). GL premium freight is $1,729-$31,223/yr (q76). Interpretation: I expect this to be fine. Testing confirms the pass-through, and leaves only the question of whether expedites the shop caused should be billed to customers at all (a goodwill cost).
hypotheses.dollars_rough: Sized from queries: likely about $0. The ceiling is GL premium freight of up to $31,223/yr (q76) if it is not recovered.
hypotheses.support: Invoices with freight below shipment freight, or GL premium freight growing beyond billed expedited freight, especially in 2016 and 2021.
hypotheses.weaken: Exact freight pass-through on all 77,077 invoices, with GL premium freight small and not tied to unbilled shipments.
